claims.text: Good facilitation gives the conversation a clear structure and then lets the customer do most of the talking.

claims.text: Glean's Visioning playbook asks for an open, consultative, and strategic tone, and warns against checklist-style or interrogative discovery. In practice: Open by stating the purpose, the agenda, the decision you need, and the time. Assign roles: a facilitator, a note-taker, a timekeeper, and a technical owner for capability questions. Use open questions and play back what you heard so it can be corrected. Make the work visible: effort-and-impact tables, a whiteboard, and sample scenarios.
claims.checked_by: Fact Integrity Auditor (studio spot check)
claims.excerpt: Set an open, consultative, and strategic tone—avoid checklist-style or interrogative discovery.
claims.note: 1 of 1 excerpt(s) matched the source text verbatim (verify-quotes, 2026-10-21).

claims.text: Ask the question, then let the customer answer it. Paraphrase what they said instead of reframing it into a product requirement. Don't treat silence or politeness as agreement. Boundary Don't commit to features, timelines, or roadmap items during a workshop. Capture capability questions for the right technical owner.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Neutral facilitation protects the evidence. Leading questions get you agreement, not information. Leading Open Wouldn't agents make this faster? What slows this process down today? This is your biggest problem, right? Which problem costs the most, and why? You'd use this every day? When did this last happen, and what did you do?

claims.text: The loudest voice in the room isn't always the best evidence. Structure the session so that every relevant role contributes.

claims.text: Glean's Visioning playbook recommends small sessions, ideally one to three participants, to encourage candor and focus, with additional sessions by line of business if needed. When a larger group can't be avoided: Use structured turns, so each role answers the same question. Ask for silent writing before discussion. Invite specific roles: "What does this look like for a new agent?" Run separate, role-specific follow-ups.
claims.checked_by: Fact Integrity Auditor (studio spot check)
claims.excerpt: Limit participant size (ideally 1-3 per session) to maximize candor and focus; run additional sessions by line of business if needed.

claims.text: A senior leader's opinion matters. It isn't the same as a front-line workflow observation, so record both and label them. When someone pulls toward their pet topic, park it visibly with an owner and return to the agenda. Boundary Never put participants on the spot about sensitive issues. Respect consent, privacy, and organizational norms.

claims.text: Acknowledge the concern. Ask what evidence would change their view. Show the assumptions, the range, and the current evidence level. Agree on a test, with an owner and a date. Boundary Don't defend an inflated number. Revise it in front of them if they're right.

claims.text: Glean's value-selling training is a reminder of why objection handling matters: assume Glean is not a budgeted initiative. When a finance leader challenges your numbers, the champion will have to answer the same challenge later, without you. Handle the objection so the champion leaves with an answer they can repeat. Acknowledge The concern is reasonable Ask What evidence would resolve it? Show The source, range, and assumptions Agree How and when it will be checked

claims.text: "Agreed. On its own, saved time is capacity, not cash. Here is what we've assumed about how much of that time is actually redeployed, and to what work. We'd propose that you or your operations owner confirm the reallocation plan, and that we measure the business metric it should move, before anyone calls it savings. Which part of the model would you want to test first?"

claims.text: Some objections are about readiness: data, security, scope, and the evaluation itself. Respond by naming the dependency and the right next step, without overpromising.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: "We're not sure our data is ready." Agree on a readiness check for the priority sources and their owners. "Security will never approve this." Engage the security owner early, and use Glean's approved security materials and review process. "Just give us a free pilot." Ask which buying question a pilot would answer, then propose the lightest validation that answers it.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Glean's pilot guide is explicit that there is no pilot without approval. A pilot requires a real sponsor, a scoped buying question, measurable criteria, readiness evidence, and internal approval. Boundary Never promise a pilot, its environment, timeline, or terms. Partners don't approve or provision pilots.

claims.text: Glean's validation-events training explains that pilots convert because the groundwork is done first: security review, the Blueprint, an economic buyer's stated priorities, executive buy-in, budget conversations, and IT readiness. Use that to reframe a pilot request. Agree on the question the pilot must answer, then show what has to be in place for the pilot to lead to a decision. Broad request Focused reframe See what it can do Answer one buying question Everyone, all content A defined cohort and data Open-ended duration Fixed duration and decision date No success criteria Measurable criteria

claims.text: Glean's onboarding training highlights a pitfall that happens before the Blueprint starts. Teams that lack confidence in the process present it as a burden, and customers decline. The fix is to position it consultatively, as a structured way to find where AI will matter most, and to show what the customer gets at the end. Apologetic pitch Positioned as a burden Endless Visioning Ideas, but no priorities DITL skipped Straight to a trial Value without baselines Numbers no one owns Readout without a decision A presentation, not a meeting Pilot without criteria A test with no path to a decision

claims.text: This is the wishlist pitfall. Run a scoring session with the business owners to select a small set of hero use cases. Each hero needs an owner, an outcome, and a target, and the rest stay in a backlog. Confirm the hero choices with the sponsor before scheduling DITL interviews.

claims.text: Blueprint engagements stall when the urgency, the sponsor, or the next step disappears. Recover by diagnosing which one is missing, not by sending more material.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Urgency: is the business problem still a priority? Has something changed? Sponsor: is the executive still engaged? Has the champion lost access or influence? Next step: is there an agreed, dated action with an owner? Evidence: is the case blocked by a missing baseline, a source, or a feasibility question?
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Re-engage the champion with a specific, useful offer, such as a short recap of the agreed priorities with a proposed next decision. Confirm or replace the sponsor path. If the priority has really changed, record that honestly. A clear "not now" is better than a false forecast. Boundary Don't flood the customer with generic content or invent urgency. Update the opportunity record accurately.
